title: Trawl Capture Management
description: Bounded packet captures from request to expiry: what was collected, how long it took, who downloaded it, and whether retention actually removed it.

panels.title: Captures by lifecycle transition
panels.description: Where captures are moving. A rise in transitions to Failed with a flat Completed line means requests are being accepted and not producing evidence.

panels.title: Capture requests by result
panels.description: Requests reaching the controller, split by how they were answered. Manual and policy-driven captures are counted separately because they fail for different reasons.

panels.title: Policy decisions
panels.description: What the armed policies decided about each event they saw. not_matched is the ordinary outcome and should dominate - the worker offers every record to every policy. The others are the story: created is a capture, duplicate collapsed onto one that already existed, rate_limited hit the hourly ceiling, disarmed is a policy that would have fired if it were armed, and failed is a qualifying event that produced no capture. No policy or rule identifier is a label here (contracts/telemetry.md), so read this for the shape and the panels below for which policy.

panels.title: Trigger source health
panels.description: 1 when the source is delivering. A policy armed against a disconnected source produces no captures and no errors, which is indistinguishable from a quiet network - this is the panel that tells them apart. suricata_loki is a query path rather than a connection, so it reflects the last poll.

panels.title: Trigger lag
panels.description: Now minus the newest event the worker has fully processed. Keeping up with quiet traffic and falling steadily behind look identical in the decision counts above; they do not look identical here.

panels.title: Trigger coverage gaps
panels.description: Coverage the worker knows it lost. A reconnect re-reads what it can; replay_window_exceeded and cursor_beyond_lookback are the reasons it could not, and both mean a window was never examined. Absence of captures over such a window is not evidence of absence of traffic (FR-039).

panels.title: Suppressed triggers
panels.description: Qualifying events that produced no new capture. duplicate is the cooldown working as intended - equivalent traffic inside one window collapses onto a single capture. rate_limited is a policy at its hourly ceiling, which recovers on its own as captures age out; sustained rate_limited means the limit is set below what the traffic produces, and captures are being missed.

panels.title: Trigger events
panels.description: Records reaching the worker. replayed is the alert query's deliberate overlap being suppressed by identity, and a rising replay rate against a flat accepted rate means the overlap is wider than it needs to be rather than that traffic increased. malformed is evidence Trawl could not store (FR-016).

panels.title: Audit ledger: policy arming and policy-created captures
panels.description: Which policy asked for which capture, and who armed it. initiatedBy names the policy behind an automatic capture; the actor is the worker's own workload identity, because the act was the worker's on the policy's behalf. This is where per-policy attribution lives - it is deliberately not a metric label, since a rule identifier as a label turns one series into as many as an operator can write.

panels.title: Reading a policy's own state
panels.description: Phase, active captures and the last suppressed trigger are per-policy state, and no policy identifier is a metric label. They live on the object, where a policy that is matching and suppressing can be told apart from one that is not matching at all.

options.content:
### Reading a policy's own state

The print columns carry phase and counts for every policy at once:

```bash
kubectl -n trawl-system get capturepolicies
```

`Phase` is `Armed`, `Disarmed`, `Degraded` or `RateLimited`. `Degraded` means
armed but not working - the tap is gone or the event source is not delivering,
so the absence of captures says nothing about the traffic.

One policy in full, including the conditions behind the phase:

```bash
kubectl -n trawl-system describe capturepolicy POLICY_NAME
```

The suppression references, which are what separate a policy that is matching
and suppressing from one that is not matching at all:

```bash
kubectl -n trawl-system get capturepolicy POLICY_NAME \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.lastTriggerTime}{"\t"}{.status.lastCaptureRef.name}{"\n"}'
```

`lastTriggerTime` moves on every matching event, including one whose capture was
suppressed. `lastCaptureRef` names the capture the event's packets are in - for a
duplicate, that is the capture it collapsed onto.

Arming a policy is a deliberate second act, recorded in the ledger above as
`capturepolicy.arm`:

```bash
kubectl -n trawl-system patch capturepolicy POLICY_NAME \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"armed":true}}'
```

panels.title: Time to first packet
panels.description: Request to CaptureStarted: scheduling the runner, pulling its image, and compiling the filter. This is the window in which the traffic under investigation is still being missed.

panels.title: Time to stored artifact
panels.description: Capture end to verified object. A failed upload that retries shows here as a long tail rather than an error, so read it alongside the artifact operations panel.

panels.title: What stopped each capture
panels.description: Captures stopping on size rather than duration are being truncated: the requested window was not fully observed, and the analyst is looking at a prefix of the traffic.

panels.title: Capture size
panels.description: Artifact sizes. Read with the bound panel: sizes pinned at the configured maximum are the same captures stopping on size.

panels.title: Artifact operations
panels.description: Upload, verify, redirect and delete against the artifact bucket. A failure series here is the bucket, not the capture path.

panels.title: Download decisions
panels.description: Every download the gateway answered, by decision. All eight decisions are pre-primed, so a flat zero line means nobody was refused rather than nothing being recorded.

panels.title: Expiry lag
panels.description: Verified deletion time minus the retention deadline. The bound is 24 hours: past that an artifact that should be gone demonstrably is not, which is a retention commitment being broken.

panels.title: Retention enforcement failures
panels.description: Retention reconciles by outcome. A sustained error series means a bucket refusing deletes, and the artifacts involved are still readable on disk while the capture says they should not be.

panels.title: Artifacts past their deadline
panels.description: Deletions that failed in the last day. Anything other than zero here is an artifact whose retention deadline has passed and whose bytes are still in the bucket.

panels.title: Audit ledger: capture and artifact records
panels.description: The ledger entries behind the panels above. This is the authoritative record: the metrics are counts, and these are the decisions.

panels.title: Downloading a capture
panels.description: How an analyst retrieves an artifact. Nothing here is a credential: the token is minted at the moment of use, scoped to this gateway, and never appears in an argument.

options.content:
### Downloading a capture

`trawlctl` runs on the analyst's workstation. Build it with `make trawlctl`.

```bash
kubectl -n trawl-system port-forward service/trawl-artifact-gateway 8443:443
```

```bash
kubectl -n trawl-system create token trawl-acceptance-analyst \
  --audience=trawl-artifact-gateway --duration=10m | \
  trawlctl capture download CAPTURE_NAME \
  --namespace trawl-system \
  --gateway https://127.0.0.1:8443 \
  --ca gateway-ca.crt \
  --token-stdin \
  --output CAPTURE_NAME.pcapng
```

The `--audience` is not optional: the gateway refuses a service account's
default token, so one cannot be replayed here to fetch packet captures.
The gateway redirects to the object store, which the workstation must be
able to reach under the hostname the redirect is signed for.

Treat the result as sensitive evidence and dispose of it through the
workstation's approved secure-file process.
